body:
## User scenario

An agent edits a project and runs a command/build. The user presses Stop, then submits another action. The embedding app needs to know that the previous command has settled, which output belongs to it, and whether it may have changed files.

## Gap in published 0.7.0

`SandboxToolchain.runBin()` accepts cwd/binPath/args and returns an exit code. It has no per-operation stop/signal or output subscription. `RuntimeController.eval()` likewise has no operation cancellation. Embedders collect global stdout/stderr themselves and implement busy state; aborting an LLM request does not stop an already-running guest command.

For shell tools, a host may additionally expose a custom worker global, wrap `FsSync` to map project-relative paths, apply readonly rules, and invoke that global through eval.

Rifty already has much of the machinery: Workbench `ProjectTerminalRun.stop()` / `ProjectRun.stop()`, and Shell options for cancellation, output chunks and mutation guards. The missing part is a coherent public no-COI SDK composition. Adding cancellation propagation from an agent remains the host's responsibility.

## Requested outcome

Expose a command/run handle with completion, stop and output tied to that invocation, or an equivalent signal-based interface. Make the existing shell usable through the same SDK worker interface with a project root and host-supplied execution/write policy.

Reuse existing command ownership and cancellation mechanisms. Do not introduce an LLM orchestrator or a separate shell implementation. Exact interface shape is open.

## Acceptance

- Each invocation has unambiguous stdout/stderr, exit/failure and cancellation settlement.
- Stop during a command/build settles the current execution before the host starts the next operation; late output/results cannot be attributed to the next run.
- File effects already applied are reported honestly; cancellation does not imply rollback. Worker replacement or unacknowledged writes, when necessary, are explicit.
- Project-relative shell paths and configured readonly paths behave consistently with file tools. Hosts can prohibit background jobs.
- A real browser test covers run → stop → next run, failed run → successful run, and cancellation during a filesystem mutation.

Path scoping and readonly policy are convenience/operation constraints, not a security-isolation claim for arbitrary guest JavaScript. Model providers, prompts, tool schemas and the user-facing Stop button stay with the embedder. Findings are based on a static audit of published 0.7.0.
title: No-COI SDK: cancellable project commands with per-run output and settlement
